The question of whether brain-training games improve cognition is genuinely contested among researchers and experts. On one side, a randomized control trial cited in [d2] found that playing Brain Age for 15 minutes per day, five times per week for four weeks produced "significant improvements in executive functions, working memory, and processing speed" in both young and elderly adults. Similarly, [d5] references an analysis by Benoit Bediou and colleagues (Psychological Bulletin) showing that "even 10-30 hours of video play significantly improved performance on tests of perception, attention, spatial cognition, and cognitive flexibility." On the other side, [d6] — drawing on neurology experts including a Washington University professor — states that "there's no strong evidence to support widespread faith in the value of word games and other brain enhancement products," with the strongest evidence for cognitive acuity pointing instead to aerobic exercise. Reinforcing this skepticism, [d7] cites the Global Council on Brain Health concluding that "the evidence today regarding the benefits of what most people consider 'brain games' is weak to non-existent," and that companies promoting these games often exaggerate their claims, though the Council does acknowledge that broadly cognitively stimulating activities can provide some benefit over a lifetime.
